title: Did Archibald James marry Elizabeth Breakey, and was little Archie their son?
desc: The narrator's central puzzle. The diary and Eliza Nelson's letters imply a marriage, but "there is no record of that marriage" {q:170} {q:T2:71}; the narrator says only that "there is no record at that date" (1823) {q:T2:68}, while affirming in both transcripts that Archibald "made the mistake of marrying that girl" {q:130} {q:T2:58}. That little Archie was the son of Archibald and Elizabeth Brakey is "believed, but not conclusively proven" {q:108} {q:T2:50}. A compiled genealogy adds a marriage of Archibald James Somerville to an Elizabeth Crawford on 30 November 1836, and a son Bellingham Brooke born in St Louis in 1852 {s:winters-p67} {s:winters-p68}; both details come from an online tree and the IGI and have not been checked. The narrator connects the question to the dormant baronetcy {q:174} {q:T2:73}.
alternatives: Married to Elizabeth Brakey (perhaps irregularly or abroad); Archie legitimate
Not married to her; Archie acknowledged by his grandparents but illegitimate
The 1836 "Elizabeth Crawford" marriage is the same union, recorded later or under another surname
The 1836 marriage is to a different woman, a later family that settled in America
next: Church of Ireland and Presbyterian registers for Ballybay/Monaghan 1822–24; the original record behind the 1836 Crawford marriage; St Louis records for Bellingham Brooke Somerville; re-read the diary and the Nelson letters.

title: Who was the eighth son of Captain William and Eliza?
desc: "Eight boys and two girls" {q:84, 96} {q:T2:40}, but only seven sons are named in the recording. A compiled genealogy (quoting an Ancestry tree) lists an eighth: Tenison, born 10 and died 22 August 1812 {s:winters-p67}. {int}This fits the narrator's account of names being reused after a child died, since the next son was Tenison Alan (1815). Still needs a baptism or burial record.
alternatives: Named in the Crisp's entry but not read out
The count of eight is a slip
next: Find the 1812 baptism or burial; read the full Crisp's pedigree.

title: Tenison or Tennyson?
desc: Both transcripts write "Tennyson" {q:14} {q:T2:7}, the speech-to-text default for the spoken name, so they are no evidence of the spelling. Eliza Bellingham's mother was Elizabeth Tenison and her brother Henry Tenison Bellingham {s:lf-bellingham}, and a compiled genealogy uses "Tenison Alan Somerville" throughout {s:winters-p67}. Tenison is very probably right; an original record would confirm it.
next: Confirm from Constabulary records or his marriage entry.

title: When, and through whom, did Tenison get his Constabulary appointment?
desc: Tenison returned in 1840 {q:204} {q:T2:83}; the narrator credits Sir William Somerville as Chief Secretary {q:212-214} {q:T2:86-87}, but Sir William held that office only from July 1847 {s:wp-1st-baron}. A compiled genealogy records two of Tenison's sons baptised at St Paul's, Trinidad, in 1842 and 1845 {s:winters-p68}, which suggests he went back to the West Indies after his marriage ("they were always looking for appointments, particularly in the West Indies" {q:T2:83}) and joined the Constabulary later.
next: RIC/Irish Constabulary officer registers (National Archives UK, HO 184) for Tenison's date of appointment.

title: The other children of Tenison and Eliza O'Connor
desc: The narrator mentions only Bellingham Arthur and an unnamed elder brother, also in the RIC {q:12} {q:T2:6}, and then moves straight to Bellingham Arthur's own children {q:216-218} {q:T2:88}. A compiled genealogy citing the IGI lists six children: William Dennistoun (1842), Tenison Alan (1845–55), Erina Bellingham (1852), Bellingham Arthur (1853), and twins Tenison Alan and Henry Bellingham (1859) {s:winters-p68}. {int}The elder brother in the RIC is probably William Dennistoun; unverified.
next: RIC officers' registers (HO 184) for William Dennistoun Somerville; Dublin baptismal registers.

title: Is the 1887 "District Inspector Somerville" Bellingham Arthur?
desc: Hansard names only "District Inspector Somerville" (24 March 1887) and "Sub-Inspector Summerville" (10 May 1887) {s:hansard-1887} {s:hansard-1887c}; the local history gives no first name {s:ballymacoda-1887}. The family's story matches closely: an RIC detachment from Cork, a dead rioter named Hanlon, a blade, arrest, Parliament, and reinstatement without a formal acquittal {q:312-322} {q:T2:118-127}, which is just what the 10 May reply describes. The narrator remembered "the 1880s", "Captain" Somerville and a fishing dispute.
next: RIC officers' registers (HO 184) for D.I. Somerville's full name and stations in 1887; Cork Examiner and Freeman's Journal reports of the March 1887 inquest; the July 1887 Cork Assizes report.

title: Captain William's regiments
desc: Family tradition: South Cork Light Infantry, "allegedly", or perhaps North Cork; "searches have been made in the military records" without success {q:54-56} {q:T2:27-28}. His later militia regiment is clear in transcript B, "the Louth, that's the County Louth Militia" {q:T2:29}, where A garbles it {q:56}; a compiled genealogy agrees {s:winters-p67}. The regular regiment remains unconfirmed.
alternatives: A regular regiment of the line
next: Militia officer lists in the Army Lists c. 1795–1830.

title: Captain William: born 1776 or 1777?
desc: Narrator: 1777, "I think" {q:62} {q:T2:30}. Published Bellingham genealogy: 1776 {s:lf-bellingham}; compiled genealogy: 3 March 1776 {s:winters-p67}.

title: Who was "Sir William Somerville the younger" at Ardrass?
desc: "Sir William Somerville the Younger inherited the house. Ardras? We don't know. I don't know. I suspect he did. Ardras continued, not in the possession of the Somerville family" {q:T2:44} {q:90}. It is unclear who "Sir William the Younger" is: perhaps a member of the senior (baronet) line, or a confusion with Captain William.
next: NLI Registered Pedigree of the Somervilles of Ardrass {s:nli-ardrass}.

title: Who sold Castle Bellingham to Sir William: Alan or his widow?
desc: Narrator: Alan "sold it, actually, to his uncle" {q:36}. Published genealogy: Alan rented it to Sir William, and Monique sold the freehold by c. 1824, after Alan's death in 1821 {s:lf-bellingham}. Both agree that it passed to the uncle.

title: The cousin in Canada who gave family members "a leg up"
desc: Transcript B clarifies A's garbled "regiment law for sale": "there was a cousin who was a regimental officer in Canada and he appears in the records as being, as giving a leg up to a number of family members" {q:T2:15-16} {q:30-34}; and "one of the Bellinghams was a descendant of an early settler in Canada" {q:T2:17}. The cousin is not identified. Monique's family, the Bâbys, were early settlers of Detroit, which may be what is meant.

title: Was Dorothea or Eliza the eldest sister?
desc: Narrator: "Dorothea being Eliza's eldest sister" {q:144} {q:T2:63-64}. Published genealogy: Elizabeth b. 1779, Dorothea b. c. 1780, though Dorothea married first (1798) {s:lf-bellingham}.

title: Clonmel, and where Archibald took ship
desc: Transcript B settles the reading: he "spent a few days in Clonmel, and then taken ship" {q:T2:65}, where A has "include Mal" {q:148}. His aunt Dorothea Riall lived in Clonmel {s:lf-bellingham}. The port of embarkation (Clonmel is inland) is not stated.

title: The house called "Farm"
desc: Transcript B: "another house called Farm, just called Farm, F-A-R-M, near Bell Turbot in County Cavan" {q:T2:77}; A garbles the place {q:182}. Belturbet, Co. Cavan is now secure; the house itself has not been located.
next: Griffith's Valuation and townland indexes around Belturbet.

title: Locate Cumry, Co. Monaghan
desc: Spelled out by the narrator as C-U-M-R-Y, which both transcripts preserve (B renders the word itself as "Cymru") {q:136} {q:T2:62}; near Ballybay {q:162} {q:T2:68}. Not yet found in townland indexes.
next: Search townlands.ie and Griffith's Valuation for Ballybay parish.

title: Tenison's Dublin address: "Livingston" or "Leinster" Avenue?
desc: Transcript A: "Livingston Avenue. Breath of Hines" {q:216}; transcript B: "Linster Avenue. Brathmines" {q:T2:87-88}. Leinster Road is in Rathmines {s:wp-rathmines}; Leinster Avenue is in North Strand, near the family's earlier home in Bayview Avenue {s:dublish-leinster-ave}.
next: Thom's Directory entries for T. A. Somerville, 1850–1895.

title: Bellingham Arthur's boyhood nickname
desc: Transcript B is clear: "As a boy, he was known as Fighting Atty. Atty being Arthur" {q:T2:12}; transcript A has "fighting atte" {q:24}. ("Artie" would sound the same.)

title: First name of the daughter who married Edmund Truell
desc: Vere. Transcript B names her three times ("Vere Demerly … the name Vere"; "Then the next sister, Vere. Vere married the second son") {q:T2:89-90} {q:T2:98}; A garbles the name as "there to money" {q:224}. A compiled genealogy citing The Times gives Vere Frances de Merlie Bellingham Somerville (1890–1976), married 14 August 1912 {s:winters-p68}.

title: Henry Rook: surname and relationship
desc: Transcript B: "Henry Rook"; A: "Henry, Rock" and "Henry Oak" {q:232-234} {q:T2:94}. Both transcripts break the sentence as "who was actually her father. That's [Bellingham] Arthur's solicitor", which must mean her father's solicitor, since he was "years older" and her husband. Rook (or Rooke) is the likeliest surname.
next: A 1912 Dublin marriage record.

title: Aunt Eddie's husband: "Uncle John" or "Uncle Jordan"?
desc: Transcript A: "Uncle Jordan", "stationed in India for that part of his career" {q:256-260}; transcript B: "Uncle John", "stationed in India for the whole of his career … years older than Eddie" {q:T2:102-103}. A compiled genealogy notes a 1929 Times notice for Edeline {s:winters-p68}, perhaps her marriage.
next: The Times, 1929; Army Lists (Royal Engineers).

title: Who commanded at Archangel, and in which regiment?
desc: Narrator: Bunt, "in the Royal Lancaster Regiment", commanded a troop sent to Archangel {q:364} {q:T2:144-145}; Jim was "a gunner, Royal Artillery" {q:366} {q:T2:145}. A war-diary-based history: "Lt. Col. W A T B Somerville DSO (Royal Artillery)" commanded the 8th (Special) Battalion MGC from 12 April 1919 {s:mgc-8bn}. A compiled genealogy citing The Times: Bunt a Lieutenant Colonel of the King's Own; Jim "Lieutenant Colonel, DSO, Royal Artillery" {s:winters-p68} {s:winters-p69}. Either the published commander's initials or his regiment and DSO are wrong, or Bunt transferred.
next: Army Lists 1918–19; the London Gazette for the DSO citation; the 8th Bn MGC war diary (WO 95).

title: Pat's capture, escapes and camps
desc: Narrator: captured "in the retreat from Mons"; escaped three times, the third successfully, across Germany and Holland; MC {q:442-450} {q:T2:170-173}. The family has camp photographs and an "article" about the escape {q:452} {q:T2:173-175}. Other accounts: Captain Gualter Somerville, 2nd Bn Royal Warwickshire Regiment, Ströhen camp, nine escape attempts (TheGenealogist, search results) {s:genealogist-pow}; captured at Zonnebeke near Ypres in October 1914, escaped 1917 (an article based on interviews with the narrator) {s:clarke-sense-of-duty}; MC 1919 (IWM, search results) {s:iwm-gualter}. The 2nd Battalion arrived only in October 1914 {s:wp-royal-warwick}.
next: National Archives (UK) WO 339 officer file; ICRC 1914–18 prisoner archive; London Gazette 1919 MC entry; the family's article and photographs.

title: "Gunners Venture" in Kenya
desc: "A company called Gunner's Venture … started by Gunner officers after the First World War who wanted a job" {q:T2:193} {q:498-500}. No independent record found yet under that name.

title: "Green desert" near Bantry
desc: Both transcripts hear "Green desert" {q:374} {q:T2:147}. A compiled genealogy citing The Times gives Bunt's death at Reendesert Lodge, Bantry {s:winters-p69}, so the place is evidently Reendesert. Still to check: the Times notice itself and the house's location.

title: Where is Uncle Jim buried?
desc: Transcript B: "he's buried in Rathnew" {q:T2:151}; transcript A: "buried in Matthew" {q:388}. Rathnew is the likelier reading; the grave has not been located.
next: Rathnew (Church of Ireland) burial register, 1950.

title: When was Clermont sold?
desc: "By the time it was all finished, it was about 1950", followed by a fragment both transcripts garble: "253" (A) and "2.53" (B) {q:566} {q:T2:224-225}. Perhaps "'52, '53", but that is a reading, not a fact. A heritage summary gives c. 1955 and the religious order came in 1956 {s:wicklowheritage-clermont} {s:irishaesthete-clermont}.

title: Was Kitty Harrison previously married to Alan Ferguson?
desc: "She married, or she had married, an Australian called Alan Ferguson" {q:374} {q:T2:146-147}. A compiled genealogy citing The Times confirms a marriage to Alan Campbell Ferguson before 1920 and to Bunt about 1925 {s:winters-p69}. Whether Ferguson died or the marriage ended in divorce is not recorded.

title: The Johnson ancestry
desc: From the interviewer's Ancestry tree, read aloud: Honor's father Philip (the Rector of Wicklow), whom the narrator confirms ("Philip was my grandfather" {q:T2:203}); his father Samuel Johnson, also confirmed {q:T2:203}; then "Zachariah" or "Samuel the Elder", and a Frances Tench, both unconfirmed {q:520-524} {q:T2:203-206}.
next: Clergy of Dublin and Glendalough succession lists for the Rectors of Wicklow; Church of Ireland records.

title: "William P. … William J." in the online tree
desc: The interviewer reads out entries ("William Henry, son of William J … I have William P, who is father of William J. William P being William Padlew") {q:118-120} {q:T2:53} that cannot be matched to anyone in the narrator's account.

title: Whose deaths prompted the destruction of the diary?
desc: Both transcripts agree on the wording: "following the death of my great-grandparents, that's my Aunt Eddie's parents, the end of the 19th century" {q:134} {q:T2:60-61}. So this is a slip in the testimony, not a transcription error. Eddie's parents died in 1916 and 1949; the narrator's great-grandparents (Tenison and Eliza, Eddie's grandparents) died around 1890–95 {q:T2:88}. We read "parents" as "grandparents".

title: Date of the recording
desc: Transcript A's file is labelled "27 Oct at 16-17"; transcript B's file is stamped "2026-10-27 19.50.34". The narrator, born 1937, is "coming up to 90" {q:50} {q:T2:25}. Everything points to 27 October 2026, but file timestamps record when the files were made, not necessarily the conversation.

title: Where are the original papers?
desc: The recording refers to Bellingham Arthur's six volumes {q:6} {q:T2:3}; his office and personal diaries, which the narrator owns {q:T2:133}; transcripts of Captain William's diary {q:132} {q:T2:59-60}; Eliza's letter about Henry {q:52} {q:T2:25-26}; the Nelson correspondence {q:166} {q:T2:69}; the Crisp's entry {q:124} {q:T2:54-55}; portraits of Dorothea and Monique and a miniature of Henry {q:26-28} {q:36} {q:44} {q:T2:13} {q:T2:18} {q:T2:22}; Pat's camp photographs and an article about his escape {q:452} {q:T2:173-175}; Reginald's Kenya photographs {q:504} {q:T2:196}; and Monique's booklet {q:42} {q:T2:21}. Cousin Eliza began photographing the portraits {q:46} {q:T2:23}. An inventory, with scans linked from this archive, is the most valuable next step.

title: "For 19 years": the family's time in Monaghan, or Archibald's age?
desc: Transcript B: "At the time, Captain William and Eliza were living in County Monaghan for 19 years" {q:T2:51}. Transcript A: "At the time. Captain, William and Eliza. Were living. About 19 years. Archibald James. And, Next brother" {q:110-112}, which could mean Archibald was about 19 (as he was in 1823 {q:T2:9}). Without the audio, both readings remain.

title: Whose servant was Elizabeth Brakey?
desc: Transcript A: "a servant girl in some household" {q:110}; transcript B: "a servant girl in the Somerville household" {q:T2:51}. The difference matters to how the family story is told, and only the audio could settle it.

title: When did Tenison Alan Somerville die, and who died first?
desc: Transcript B: "they lived there until he died first. I think about 1890. Early 1890s. She died about 1895" {q:T2:88}; A is garbled ("about 189…") {q:216}. A compiled genealogy gives Tenison's death as 31 July 1895 {s:winters-p67} and none for his wife. Either the narrator's order of deaths or the online date is wrong.
next: GRO death index (Dublin), 1888–1896, for Tenison and Cecelia Eliza Somerville.

title: Bellingham Arthur's birth: 1853 or 1856?
desc: Narrator: "born in 18… It's the year of the Crimean War, anyway. I think it was 1856" {q:T2:1-2} {q:2}. IGI, via a compiled genealogy: born 17 November 1853, baptised in Dublin 16 June 1854 {s:winters-p68}. The Crimean War (1853–56) fits both years.
next: The 1854 Dublin baptismal register; RIC officer register (which records date of birth).

title: Rachel: Margaret's sister or her mother?
desc: The narrator: Margaret's elder sister and co-heiress was "Rachel" {q:330} {q:T2:131}. A compiled genealogy names Margaret's mother as Rachel Hall Wright {s:winters-p68}. Both could be true.

title: Where was Reginald's Kenya farm?
desc: "Eventually his mother bought a farm … a thatched hut … he built it up"; transcript B adds "a long way from Nanyuki" {q:T2:196-197}, where A has "Long way from UK" {q:504}.

title: Maudie Moore: "from Greystokes"?
desc: Transcript B: "he married a girl from Greystokes called Maudie Moore. She came from the County Laois family" {q:T2:197}; A: "grace studs … Morde Moore … County leash family" {q:506-508}. Greystones, Co. Wicklow is a guess, and her formal first name is not recorded.
next: The 1928 marriage record (Ireland or Kenya); Kenya Gazette notices.

title: What killed Bellingham Arthur in 1916?
desc: "He died, unfortunately, in 1916 of the flu that was then going around in the First World War"; asked if it was the Spanish flu, the narrator says "I always thought that he died of the Spanish flu, but … was that just after the First World War?" {q:10-12} {q:T2:4-5}. The 1918–19 pandemic came later {s:dcc-flu}, so it was not the Spanish flu as usually dated. What illness it was (influenza or something else) is unconfirmed. A compiled genealogy gives the date of death as 20 January 1916 {s:winters-p68}.
next: The civil death certificate (Rathnew/Wicklow registration district, January 1916).

title: Who, if anyone, is heir to the dormant Somerville baronetcy?
desc: The baronetcy became dormant when the 2nd Baron Athlumney died childless on 8 January 1929 {q:174} {q:T2:73} {s:wp-2nd-baron}. The narrator raises it to explain why Archibald's marriage matters {q:174} {q:T2:73}. This archive does not assess any claim. A claimant must prove legitimate male-line descent from a baronet, so the open points include: whether the senior line (from Quaile) has any surviving male heirs; whether Major William was a son of the 1st Baronet, as the narrator and a compiled genealogy say {s:winters-p66}; whether Archibald James was lawfully married and has male-line descendants (the 1852 St Louis birth of Bellingham Brooke Somerville is one lead {s:winters-p68}); and the male lines of Corry, Tenison Alan and his sons.

title: Reginald's birth year
desc: Both transcripts: "My father was 17 when the Great War started in 1914" {q:348} {q:T2:138}, and "He was 38 at the time" (about 1934) {q:510} {q:T2:199}. Those imply 1896–97, but no record has been found.
